---
title: "Singular fits"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

The [random-effects-correlation page](random-effect-correlations.qmd) represented intercept and slope deviations with a covariance matrix. A [**singular fit**](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/isSingular.html) occurs when the estimated covariance matrix has lower rank than the formula allows.

We first connect rank to covariance dimensions, then fit a predeclared MALD stress test, inspect the collapsed direction, and separate singularity from optimizer convergence.

## Rank and covariance dimensions

Suppose a grouping term requests $q$ random-effect dimensions with covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$. A nonsingular fit requires

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)=q.
$$

Writing the eigendecomposition as

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma
=\mathbf Q\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf Q^{\mathsf T},
$$

the rank is the number of positive eigenvalues in $\boldsymbol\Lambda$. If one eigenvalue is zero, one linear combination of the requested deviations has no fitted variation and

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)<q.
$$

In a two-dimensional intercept-slope model, singularity can arise when a variance reaches zero or when the correlation reaches an endpoint. In a larger structure, a collapsed dimension may involve a combination of several terms and may not be obvious from any one printed variance.

## Fitting a predeclared MALD stress test

The stress-test model asks participants to vary in an intercept, frequency slope, duration slope, trial-order slope, and frequency-by-duration interaction slope. It also gives words a trial-order slope. The fixed interaction remains in both models because the diagnostic concerns the group covariance structure.

Before fitting, the design audit asks whether each requested slope's predictor varies within its group. Frequency, duration, trial order, and their frequency-by-duration product vary within participants. Trial order varies within words because the same word occurs at different points for different participants. This support is necessary, but it does not guarantee that the data estimate all variances and correlations away from a boundary.

```{r}
#| label: mald-singular
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

standardize <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(scale(x))
}

mald$z_frequency <- standardize(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$z_duration <- standardize(mald$log_duration)
mald$z_trial <- standardize(mald$trial_order)

fit_control <- lmerControl(
  optimizer = "bobyqa",
  optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
)

overfit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency * z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency * z_duration + z_trial | participant_id) +
    (1 + z_trial | item),
  data = mald,
  control = fit_control
)

revised <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency * z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial | participant_id) +
    (1 + z_trial | item),
  data = mald,
  control = fit_control
)

singularity_check <- c(
  interaction_slope_model = isSingular(overfit, tol = 1e-4),
  revised_model = isSingular(revised, tol = 1e-4)
)
singularity_check
```

`isSingular(..., tol = 1e-4)` declares a fitted covariance direction effectively zero relative to the fitted scale at that numerical tolerance. It is a diagnostic, not a theorem about the population. A different tolerance can change a borderline flag, so the rotated standard deviations below remain part of the evidence.

The model requesting participant interaction-slope variation is singular. Removing only that unsupported random slope gives the prespecified nonsingular revision. This comparison does not remove the fixed frequency-by-duration interaction or the item trial-order slope.

## Inspecting the fitted dimensions

`rePCA()` rotates each fitted covariance matrix into orthogonal directions. The returned standard deviations are the square roots of the rotated, residual-scaled eigenvalues.

```{r}
#| label: mald-singular-dimensions
overfit_sd <- rePCA(overfit)$participant_id$sdev
revised_sd <- rePCA(revised)$participant_id$sdev

dimension_table <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    model = "Interaction slope requested",
    dimension = seq_along(overfit_sd),
    orthogonal_sd = overfit_sd
  ),
  data.frame(
    model = "Interaction slope removed",
    dimension = seq_along(revised_sd),
    orthogonal_sd = revised_sd
  )
)
dimension_table
```

The final participant direction in the larger model collapses to the boundary. Because the rotated directions are linear combinations, this fact is stronger than merely inspecting whether one named standard deviation looks small.

```{r}
#| label: singularity-plot
ggplot(
  dimension_table,
  aes(x = factor(dimension), y = orthogonal_sd)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, fill = "grey55") +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  labs(
    x = "Participant covariance dimension",
    y = "Orthogonal SD (residual-scaled)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Separating singularity from convergence

An optimizer can reach a boundary optimum successfully, producing a singular fit without a convergence failure. Conversely, a nonsingular covariance estimate can accompany an optimizer warning. `isSingular()` and the optimizer diagnostics answer different questions and both should be checked.

`bobyqa` is used because the stress test has many bounded covariance parameters; `maxfun = 200000` gives that optimizer more evaluations than its default. <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting --> Neither choice adds information to the design. A boundary estimate concerns the fitted optimum, a convergence warning concerns whether the optimizer reached an adequate optimum, and nonidentifiability concerns whether distinct parameter values imply indistinguishable behavior. These problems may coincide, but they are not synonyms.

A singular fit should send us back to the design: which predictor contrasts vary within which groups, how many group levels support the covariance, and which population variation the scientific claim requires. Plausible responses include removing an unsupported correlation, removing an unsupported slope, collecting more within-group contrasts, or using a regularized model. These moves encode different population assumptions.

The decision sequence is: (i) inventory within-group contrasts before fitting, (ii) inspect convergence and rank separately, (iii) identify the collapsed covariance direction, (iv) apply the prespecified revision tied to the scientific target, and (v) refit and report the changed population assumption. The MALD revision removes only the collapsed participant interaction slope. It is not a general stepwise-selection recipe, and it should not be used to search for a preferred fixed-effect conclusion.

## Recap and check

1. Does a singular fit necessarily mean optimizer failure? No. The optimizer may successfully locate a boundary optimum.
2. Does increasing `maxfun` repair an unsupported random slope? No. It changes the computational budget, not the information in the design.

The [next page](generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd) carries the same group-variation logic to a binary linguistic response.
